label: Sharples (2008): the near-modern free-will problem in Alexander's De Fato is a historiographical 'accident/coincidence' of two independently-developing strands (RDS + PEA)
description: Sharples' mature retrospective ('L'accident du déterminisme', 2008) half-recants his 1983 'Laplacian/retrospective-history' framing. He ASSERTS that the appearance of a near-modern free-will problem in Alexander's De Fato is, most economically, a 'coincidence'/'irony of history' — the independent convergence of a reformulated Stoic determinism (RDS, ~Philopator) and a Peripatetic equal-possibility doctrine (PEA). He broadly endorses Bobzien's 'inadvertent' framework while contesting RDS<->PEA priority and dating two-sided possibility earlier (Epicurus, Carneades). Page anchor: pp. 289-301, esp. 301: 'RDS et PEA … se soient développés vers la même époque … relève, en quelque sorte, de la coïncidence' [tr.: '…is, in a sense, a matter of coincidence']. Ancient locus: De Fato ch. 13 ~= Nemesius NH 34 (102-103 Morani); In An. Pr. I.13 162.1-163.23. Modern labels ('libertarian','determinism') are Sharples' own analytic categories.

metadata.lang_note: French source quoted verbatim; English is a marked translation

label: Blackson: Frede mis-specifies the object of choice — adults choose to EXERCISE the ability to use impressions (E), not choose to ASSENT (D); on E, the early Stoics probably already had a notion of a will
description: Blackson ASSERTS that Frede's 'minimum belief' for a Stoic notion of a will misidentifies the object of choice. Frede's proposition D: adults choose to assent to impulsive impressions. Blackson's proposition E: adults choose to exercise the ability to use impressions, with assent the downstream outcome. Epictetan passages (Disc. II.18.23-26; Manual 34; Disc. I.28.2) support E. Conclusion (p.100): if E is correct, 'the early Stoics probably believed E too', making the first notion of a will pre-Epictetan and Frede 'very likely wrong' that it is a late-Stoic innovation. Epictetus introduced prohairesis for pedagogical/social reasons — 'more of a gifted teacher than a philosophical innovator' (p.96). HEDGED ('probably'; limited to best-known passages). Page anchors: 83-84, 90-92, 96, 99-100. NB: this complements the existing shell scholarly_argument_blackson_early_stoics_on_will_and_choic_2 with the explicit D-vs-E contrast and the anti-Frede conclusion.

metadata.claim: Karamanolis EXPLICITLY 'side[s] with Bobzien (1998a,1998b) and Frede (2011) against Dihle (1982)' (ch.4 n.15, p.162): the will-concept is absent from Plato/Aristotle and emerges in the Hellenistic schools.
Karamanolis aligns with Frede: the will-vocabulary (to eph'hēmin, prohairesis, autexousion) is 'of Stoic provenance' (p.133); Christians inherit Epictetus' prohairesis as their notion of will.
Karamanolis explicitly against Dihle: the will-concept is 'conspicuously absent from Plato and Aristotle' and is a Stoic import, NOT a late Christian/Augustinian invention.

metadata.re_anchor: Karamanolis (pp.142-143): patristic autexousion BREAKS with Stoic compatibilist eleutheria by adopting the Peripatetic/Platonist two-sided (X-or-Y) conception. Re-anchors his Debate-D position to the Christian-autexousion concept.

metadata.claim: THE fault-line. AGREE the early Stoa lacked free will. DISAGREE on what comes next: Frede (Epictetus HIMSELF = 'our first actual notion of a free will', p.77) vs Bobzien (a will-faculty enters only later, in Platonist/Christian theological determinism; Epictetus' prohairesis only an INFLUENCE — 1998 p.173 / 2001 p.412 'Alexander stops short of a concept of free will').
metadata.reconstructed: Clash is real but staged ACROSS the two books — Frede 2011 postdates/partly responds to Bobzien; Bobzien 2001 does not name Frede as the chs.6-8 antagonist.

metadata.claim: Blackson contests Frede's timeline from the OPPOSITE direction to Bobzien: not 'did Epictetus invent it?' but 'the EARLY Stoics probably already had it' — Frede wrong on both ends under Blackson's E-reading.

metadata.re_anchor: Blackson directly responds to Frede's schema of the will (his propositions C/D), substituting proposition E. Re-anchors to the Frede-schema concept node.

metadata.claim: Frede states his aim is 'completely different from Dihle's' (p.6) and displaces the origin of the will from Augustine BACK to Epictetus. Dihle: 'the notion of will … was invented by St. Augustine' (p.123).

Sorabji 2017 ('Freedom and Will: Graeco-Roman Origins', Selfhood and the Soul, OUP, pp.49-67): the idea of the will has four strands (rationality, freedom, power/'will power', perversion by pride) assembled only in Augustine; NONE of the four as a cluster is in Epictetus (pp.62-63). Direct rebuttal of Frede's POLE 2.

metadata.claim: Kahn 1988 (pp.235-259) is multi-causal: against Dihle's biblical-only account (p.259) AND any single-source 'Epictetus decisive' account. The will is 'discovered' on an overdetermined trajectory: Chrysippus' sunkatathesis -> Latin voluntas (Lucretius earliest libera voluntas p.248) -> Epictetus' prohairesis -> Augustine.

metadata.claim: Kahn and Frede AGREE Aristotle has no unified will-concept (Kahn p.241: the four notions eph'hēmin/hekousion/prohairesis/boulēsis are 'conceptually independent'; Frede p.28). They disagree on single- vs multi-causal origin.

metadata.claim: Irwin 1992 (p.467) + Aquinas: Aristotle ALREADY has a concept of the will (boulēsis = essentially rational desire); intellectualism-vs-voluntarism is a dispute between two views of a SHARED concept, not a late invention. Opposes Frede's 'no will in Aristotle' (p.28).

metadata.claim: Irwin (with Kenny) rejects the 'late invention' premise shared by Dihle and Frede; Aristotle already has the concept. 2007 leg: Augustine too is an intellectualist compatibilist, NOT a voluntarist inventor (§224 p.411).

Sorabji 1980 (Necessity, Cause and Blame, pp.244-247): against the orthodoxy (incl. Huby 'first discovery of the free-will problem' 1967), Aristotle DID see the determinism/responsibility clash; the Hellenistic novelty was the Stoics' PERSISTENCE in determinism, 'not the invention of determinism, nor the realisation that determinism clashed' (p.247). Distinct from his 2017 four-strands essay.
metadata.note: Debate-A/Aristotle-indeterminism thesis (1980 book) — DISTINCT from the 2017 four-strands (Debate B). Keep the two Sorabji works separate.

metadata.claim: Bobzien's decisive contrast: one-sided causative (Stoic — mere causal responsibility) vs two-sided potestative (Peripatetic — power for opposites). Both concept nodes already exist; this edge makes the contrast explicit.

metadata.claim: M. Frede (p.100): Alexander is the 'ancestor' of the do-otherwise notion but 'not able to provide a coherent account' of it (two confusions: misunderstood Stoic determinism; mistaken notion of merit, pp.100-101). A confused dead-end, not Bobzien's inadvertent way-station.

Sharples 2008 broadly ENDORSES Bobzien's 'inadvertent' framework (the De Fato problem is an 'accident/coincidence' of RDS+PEA, p.301) while contesting RDS<->PEA priority and dating two-sided possibility earlier (Epicurus, Carneades).

Sharples 2008 is the mature retrospective on his own 1983 'Alexander = libertarian, not soft-determinist' thesis (p.9) — partly self-revising. Links the new 2008 argument node to the existing 1983 position shell.

Donini (ch.III, pp.74-77): Alexander 'in quite unaristotelian fashion' suppresses Aristotle's 'for the most part' frequencies to widen contingency ('reticence/distortion'). BUT his settled view (ch.VII, pp.165-176) rehabilitates the De Fato as 'substantially consistent' on a two-class (ordinary agent / phronimos) reading.
metadata.balance_flag: Fast pass presents Donini as flatly 'distortion' — add the ch.VII rehabilitation as a qualifier.

metadata.re_anchor: Amand's core thesis: a single moral anti-fatalist schema, Carneades 'sinon inventée, du moins aiguisée et popularisée' (p.IX), transmitted to the Greek Christian theologians. Re-anchors to the astrological-fate concept. Carneades' liberty = probabilist/pragmatist, NOT dogmatic (p.65).

metadata.claim: Per Amand's reconstruction (>=3/6 règle de fer, p.573), the lost Carneadean moral anti-fatalist topos precedes and feeds the surviving polemic in Philo, Alexander, Firmicus, Eusebius, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Chrysostom, Nemesius (the six témoins + confirmatory).
metadata.hedge: Amand HEDGES invention ('sinon inventée') and Alexander's verbatim dependence ('impossible de décider', p.586).

metadata.claim: CRITICAL: Amand treats Alexander as a PARALLEL WITNESS to the lost Carneadean stock, NEVER as the source of Origen (p.586). Ramelli asserts the OPPOSITE filiation: Alexander -> Origen direct inspiration. Neighbouring but NON-equivalent — must not be conflated. Citing Amand in support of Ramelli's priority would be a misattribution.

metadata.re_anchor: Frede's positive thesis: Epictetus articulates 'our first actual notion of a free will' (p.77). 'libertarian' is NOT Frede's label for his own (Stoic) view — he assigns the incoherent open-alternatives notion to Alexander (pp.100-101). Re-anchors to the Frede-schema concept.
